before: Walk the East Eagle Trail up the valley for about 1.5 mi, then leave it and head right into the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side. The line climbs the loose, steep rib that divides two prominent drainages; stay on the crest of the rib rather than in the gullies either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake. From the lake, pick up the Little Kettle Creek Trail and follow its many switchbacks back down to the East Eagle Trailhead.

The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

Also published as 'A Slave to Liberty' (450m, Grade V, 5.13-). Climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then breaks right to join Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before launching into eight new pitches (four rated 5.12) up the East Face, with the crux 5.13 slab on pitch 8. Mikey Schaefer began equipping the line in 2015 and completed a one-day free ascent, leading every pitch, in early August 2016 with Shanjean Lee's support.

Climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death (5.10, 5.11, 5.11), then a right-leaning overlap (P4, 5.12-) into a traverse with layback flakes and a mantle (P5, 5.12-), an arete with a big hand-rail traverse (P6, 5.12), a 165 ft 'mega slab' pitch with 14 bolts and 4 crux moves (P7, 5.12+), and a razor-thin slab crux (P8, 5.13-) before easing off through P9-P11 (5.10-5.10+).

before.name: Washington Pass Hairpin Turnout
before.note: This route starts from the East Face hairpin pullout, not the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the Beckey Route. Same hairpin turnout as the neighboring Kangaroo Temple routes.
before.directions: Drive SR-20 over Washington Pass and continue east a short way down to the big hairpin turn below the pass, and park off the road at the curve at about 5,100 ft. The highway over the pass is closed in winter.

before.name: Liberty Bell Mountain
before.note: True summit of Liberty Bell Mountain.
before.directions: Walk back up the road toward the pass to a pond on its south side, and from the pond's east end follow the cairned climbers' path about a mile through forest to the East Face talus. Climb the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, step right onto Thin Red Line just below its third anchor, and follow this route's eight pitches; from the top, scramble to the summit roped.

before.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the Freedom or Death ramp
before.notes:
Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

This route was equipped largely rope-solo and first freed in August 2016 and originally documented under an earlier name. It climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, then steps right onto Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before eight new pitches of its own.
hazards: No independent start; a party that mislocates Freedom or Death mislocates this route
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed for the descent
Loose talus in the upper approach
before.baseFinding:
This route does not have a start of its own. It starts on Freedom or Death, and that is the fact to carry up the talus. So the base finding is Freedom or Death's base finding: A small leftward-trending ramp just to the right of Liberty Crack, with bolts visible on the face above it.

Why that is actually useful rather than a dodge: it means you are not hunting for a fifth start among the East Face cluster. There are three pitches of shared, well-bolted climbing before this route becomes its own thing, and the decision point is up on the wall where you can see it, not down in the talus where you cannot.

The negative test: Liberty Crack is 40 ft left along third and fourth class ledges from the base of the talus. If you are scrambling left on ledges you are heading for Liberty Crack. If you have walked well right past a series of starts you are among the Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice and Independence lines.

Countable on the climb: three pitches of 5.10, 5.11 and 5.11, then a step right. If you are still going straight up after three pitches you have missed the junction with Thin Red Line.

And the descent follows Thin Red Line's, not Freedom or Death's: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge from a fixed pin and wire, then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base. Five rappels, all on bolted stations after the first.

before: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.

before.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
before.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
before.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
before.baseFinding: The dried-up tarn with cabin remnants is the proof, and the old mine on the crest confirms it. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.

before: P1-P4 and most of P5 are the standard Let It Burn line, then two pitches (5.12- and 5.11-) lead into the West Face finish. P1 (5.8): ramp to a thin splitter crack, tree belay. P2 (5.10+): another short splitter, walk left to a second tree belay. P3 (5.12-): a few 5.10 cracks past a 5.11 slot where the old fixed pin has been removed, leaving a good cam placement; crux is two bolts moving left; belay at a two-bolt anchor. P4 (5.11a): hands and fingers crack to knobs and a double crack; belay at a fixed pin and bolt. P5 (5.11+): flare crack becoming a lieback; belay on 1" gear on a rightward bench. P6 (5.12-): a difficult flake/crack sequence; belay in the chimney right of a razor flake. P7 (5.11-): tips V-slot to a roof, then a corner. P8 (5.11+): hand crack to a roof. P9 (5.10): overhanging chimneys to a large ledge. P10 (5.6): easy 300 feet to the summit.

before.belay: Stop on the flat ledge at the foot of the vertical crack, once the ramp steps are behind you.
before.notes: Shared with Let it Burn and the West Face. A few steep moves up the broken ramp system trending right, past a tree, then easier ground to a flat ledge below a vertical splitter. Grades given for this pitch range from 5.7 to 5.8.

before.belay: Walk the ledge left to its far end and belay at the trees there.
before.notes: A short thin-hands splitter, roughly 25 ft of hard climbing, then easier ground up and left along the ledge to the trees at its far left end for the belay.

before.belay: Belay at the two-bolt anchor reached after the crux finger crack and knobs.
before.notes: Finger cracks lead to a V-slot with a thin crack. The flakes on the left are detached: step on them rather than pull. Go up and right past a small roof, then traverse left past two bolts on the crux moves. Finish on knobs and a finger crack to a two-bolt belay. The old fixed pin is gone and leaves a good cam placement.

before.belay: Belay at the anchor on the small ledge at the top of the pitch.
before.notes: Hands and fingers on knobs, fins and thin cracks, stepping right twice into new crack systems, to a double crack. Belay at a fixed pin and a bolt on a small ledge.

before.belay: Belay on the narrow ledge above the overhanging flake, at the top of the pitch; the new line heads off right from there.
before.notes: Move into the right-slanting flared slot, mantle right onto a square ledge, then make a powerful layback past an overhanging flake. Near the top of this pitch Accendo Lunae leaves Let it Burn: belay on a bench to the right, on gear around 1 in.

before.belay: Belay in a small alcove just to the right of the sharp flake.
before.notes: New terrain. Traverse right, then climb a gently overhanging line of thin cracks and tips locks. The crux passes a wedged flake that flexes, so gear placements beside it are unreliable. Belay in a small alcove in the chimney just right of a razor-sharp flake. Grades for this pitch range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

New terrain. Awkward body positions up a tips crack in a V-shaped flare lead to a stance under a 4 ft roof where the corner switches from right-facing to left-facing. Good gear overhead protects a double hand-jam pull over the roof into thin hands, which fights up to a ledge. Grades given run from 5.11- to mid-5.11.
Back on the West Face for its crux: a perfect hand crack up the arching corner to an even bigger roof, surmounted on its left side to a stance. Grades range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

The West Face's overhanging chimneys. Fight past the first overhang into a squeeze chimney, exit to a crack, then into a second flaring chimney. Step right at a big block to belay on a large ledge. Originally rated 5.8, it is widely regarded as climbing like 5.10.

Easy blocky ground up and right to the summit, usually simul-climbed. A notch on the far right gives quick access to the walk-off. From the summit block a single 30 m rappel east off a slung horn reaches the descent.

before.name: Icicle Creek Road (FR 7600) to Eightmile Road / Forest Road 7601
before.status: Paved for about 8.4 mi, then roughly 4 mi of bumpy, potholed dirt on FR 7601 to the Stuart Lake Trailhead.
before.driveNote: High clearance helpful late season; parking only on the right side of FR 7601 between Eightmile Lake and the trailhead, and the lot fills before dawn on summer weekends.
before.seasonalGate: FR 7601 gated to vehicles roughly November through May; parking at the gate adds about 7 miles round trip.

before: A new route on the steep east face of South Peak featuring challenging crack and face climbing on white granite.

before.notes: Start in the large corner in the middle of the east face and climb the splitter finger and hand cracks on the wall right of the corner, up out of the moat to a ledge on the right. Good-quality climbing; this is the best pitch of the route.

Traverse right from the ledge, then follow an offwidth straight up through an overhang. The rock here is loose and dangerous, with broken chimney and dike ground; this feature is not recommended and is worth avoiding unless you want exactly that.
Easier mid-fifth-class climbing up and left to the summit.

before: Finish via the standard North Face route by traversing Burgundy Ledge to its rappel line, or continue on rambling terrain (up to 5.7) directly to the summit.

before.name: SR-20 Burgundy Col Pullout
before.note: Long unmarked pullout on the east shoulder of SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about 4 miles east of Washington Pass; the climber's trail drops down the embankment on the east side.
before.directions: From Washington Pass, drive SR-20 east about 3.75 miles, past the hairpin turn, to the next long pullout on the east shoulder near milepost 166, opposite Silver Star. The climbers' path is not signed — it drops off the east side of the embankment.

before.name: Early Winters Creek Crossing
before.note: Trail descends ~200 ft from the pullout to ford/log-cross Early Winters Creek; last reliable, easy water before the steep climb begins.
before.directions: The boot path drops down the embankment through talus and into forest, passing a register box, and loses a little over 200 ft to a log crossing of Early Winters Creek. Fill up here: this is the last easy water before the climb, with only an unreliable trickle near the col above.

before.name: The Bench
before.note: Flat forested camping bench with multiple established tent sites and views toward the Liberty Bell group; common first-night camp for a two-day trip.
before.directions: From the creek the trail turns east and climbs steeply and continuously, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in a mile and a half of forest to the flat bench. This is about the halfway point of the approach by both distance and gain, which is why parties splitting the trip camp here.

before.name: Burgundy Col
before.note: 7,770-ft notch gained via 1,000+ ft of loose ball-bearing scree; from here descend/traverse loose rock or steep snow around the north face to reach the route.
before.directions: Above the bench the ground opens into loose scree gullies, finishing with a cairned stretch of unstable scree over slab to the notch. This is the crux of the approach in both directions — the ball-bearing scree is the main hazard on the route, and the col's east side can hold snow or ice into summer.

before.name: Splitter flake start
before.note: About 5-10 minutes below the col via loose rock/snow scramble to a clean splitter flake; P1 climbs the flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left.
before.directions: Do not start climbing at the col. Scramble down and around the base of Burgundy's north face on loose rock, or on steep snow that can want an axe into midsummer, for five to ten minutes until you are directly under a clean splitter flake. The start sits about 15 ft climber's-left of Ultramega OK's twin cracks, so it is further along the base than both the North Face's start and Ultramega OK's.

before.name: Burgundy Spire Summit
before.note: Eight varied, loose and lichen-covered pitches (crux 5.10c) top out at the summit; standard descent is the North Face's 5-rappel line (double ropes) back toward the col.
before.directions: Eight pitches: a flake system to a roof pull and lieback, a right-trending finger crack, then the lichened, steep 5.10c finger crack that is the crux. Fourth-class ground trends left to a chimney, then a poor-rock corner and steep, thinly-protected bulges at 5.10 with the belay beyond the arete. The last pitch either rambles up to 5.7 past an old bolt to the skyline and the true summit, or traverses Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route — the descent is the North Face rappel line either way.

before: Doubles of cams from 0.4 in to #3 with a few smaller cams and one #4-equivalent; full nut set.
Rack doubles from 0.4-3 inches with a few smaller cams and one #4, plus a set of nuts.

before.notes: A fun flake system to a roof pull and lieback on the left; the scramble concludes at a horn wrapped in fixed webbing.
Step left to a sweet, right-trending finger crack; pull a bulge and cut hard left to a stance.

before.belay: Belay on a good ledge above the steep finger crack and spooky flakes.
before.notes: The steepest pitch: a lichen-covered finger crack up spooky flakes to a good belay ledge.
Trend left toward the chimney and belay on its left side.
A fun, mostly solid chimney; the blocks are generally sound but warrant care.

before.belay: Belay at the top of the right-facing corner.
before.notes: Poorer-quality rock requiring a left traverse to a right-facing corner.

before.belay: Belay on the far side of the arete, past the steep bulges.
before.notes: Steep bulges with just enough gear to feel heads-up in the mid-5.10 range; belay beyond the arête.
Rambling terrain, up to 5.7, to the skyline and true summit, or finish by traversing Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route.

before.pull: Keep both ends clear of the constriction above the wide crack before the last climber pulls - it is the documented rope trap on this descent.
before.notes: First rappel of the shared North Face descent line.
hazards: A single 60 m rope does NOT reach the bolts: you finish roughly 10 ft above them and downclimb easy 5th class to get there. A 70 m single is the length that reaches, and is what recent parties recommend
This is the rappel where a party got a rope end stuck in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 back up to free it
before.station: The summit anchor - the heavily slung summit boulder - dropping down the upper north face to what is reported to be the only bolted anchor on the whole rappel route. Everything below it is slung natural gear, so this is the one station you can identify with certainty.

before.notes: Traverses to reach the next anchor.
before.anchor: Bolts to a ledge near a rock arch
hazards: The line does not follow the route, so what you see going down is not what you climbed
before.station: Down toward the main ledge system. Parties on two ropes report doubling up and rappelling climber's-left of the climbing line to reach the next station rather than dropping straight down it.

before.notes: Drops to a slung horn.
hazards: Ledge-to-ledge rappelling on this face means loose material sitting on every stance above you
before.station: A single rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.

before.notes: Down to scree ledges.
hazards: You have to walk under and past a large block to find this station, so it is not visible from where the previous rappel lands
Traversing a ledge with the ropes still out is where they snag on this descent
before.station: From the ledge, cut climber's left to the station, which sits just after you walk back underneath the large block. A station is also reported at the top of pitch 4, reached by a ledge traverse - the ledge is the feature to navigate by, not the fall line.

before.notes: Final rappel back to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start.
hazards: The notch is the aiming point; below the col the descent continues down loose gullies on foot
before.station: The last rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col. From the final stance the rappel route is a straight shot through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.

before: Described as the recommended route: gain Asa Peak's Northeast Ridge, traverse to Agnes's south ridge, and climb short technical sections up to 5.6-5.8. From a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass, parties make a rising traverse over snow, talus, and slabs to the south ridge crest south of Point 7760, then rope up for several pitches of Class 4-5 rock on or left of the crest. Where the crest gets too craggy, downclimb one pitch to a ledge system and traverse to a whaleback with views of the summit block. From the 7,480-ft south col, traverse a high snowpatch and ascend a broad Class 2-3 ramp just left of a snow-filled gully, dog-legging right to a headwall; a 5.8 chimney (the crux) and one more roped pitch lead to a final ~100-ft Class 2-3 scramble to the summit.

The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on the Minidike: park 1.5 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead on the left (SE) side of the road, just after crossing a bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.

From the glacier directly below the northeast face, traverse (or first climb to near the col northwest of the peak) to reach the mixed rock and snow of the upper NE face. A large 45-degree snow gully, reached by a traverse onto the rock face, is a key feature; above it, the line moves south on pleasant, moderate rock (mostly class 3, occasional class 4), with snow patches often persisting until late summer.

before.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
before.note: Start of the High Pass Trail; Northwest Forest Pass required at the trailhead.
before.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road to its end at about 5,200 ft. The final miles are rough and deeply rutted, and many parties park short and walk them rather than risk the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; the signed High Pass Trail starts from the parking area.

before.name: High Pass
before.note: Leave the maintained trail here; drop and follow the climbers' path north and west toward the old Gargett Mine.
before.directions: About a quarter mile up, the short spur to the Winchester Mountain lookout splits off — stay north on the High Pass Trail. It contours the west side of Winchester, dips through the minor saddle known as Low Pass with open views west to Tomyhoi, then climbs steadily to High Pass. This is maintained tread the whole way, roughly 750 ft of gain; Mount Baker comes into view south when you top out.

before.name: Gargett Mine
before.note: Old mine workings; last reliable water source until lingering snow patches high on the peak. Coordinate is the surveyed mine adit (elev 5708 ft) - parties camp in the basin just below at ~5400 ft.
before.directions: Leave the maintained tread at the pass and follow the climbers' path north and west, dropping about 550 ft to the old mine workings. Tent space here is limited, so most parties bivy rather than camp properly. Fill up: the mine creek is the last easy water until lingering snow patches high on the peak.

before.name: Notch (Mt. Larrabee NW rib)
before.note: Reached after a long, unmarked sidehill traverse below Larrabee's southwest and west flanks; drop slightly beyond into the red talus/moraine bowl. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit — estimated, not surveyed.
before.directions: From the mine, traverse north across Larrabee's timbered southwest rib in the first quarter mile, then commit to a full mile of unmarked sidehill below Larrabee's west flank — steep talus, scree, heather and slick herbaceous slopes with no tread. A small scree chute at the end leads to the notch in Larrabee's rocky northwest rib. Do not start this traverse on wet grass or wet rock; helmets go on here and stay on, since rockfall is the defining hazard of the whole approach.

before.name: South AmBo Saddle
before.note: Scrambling and low 5th-class climbing begins here, below the rock feature climbers call 'De Gaulle's Nose'. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit — estimated, not surveyed.
before.directions: Beyond the notch, descend a steep dirt chute between snow and rock, then contour at roughly 5,800 ft above the moraine bowl. From there angle north through a series of steep gullies and ribs to the saddle. Route-finding, not difficulty, is what costs time on this section, and the red talus is loose throughout.

before.name: American Border Peak summit
before.note: Views to Mt. Larrabee, Canadian Border Peak, and the Pickets.
before.directions: Follow a faint climbers' path along the crest for about two hundred yards, then traverse right onto slabby red ledges near a rock rib. A cleft just left of the rib and more slabby ledges gain a flat step on top of it; a down-sloping bench then crosses to the mouth of a steep snow gully, where a tall snow fin splits the gully and you take a moat on either side or the hole through the fin itself. From the notch above, two pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top — a 5.3 entry, then a smooth 5.4 face move over a large chockstone and a squeeze so tight that packs have to be pushed through ahead of the climber. Above the chimney a dirty slabby trough, a row of horns and gaps, and one dramatically exposed step-across finish the climb.

before: Accounts disagree on the count. One party made three rappels on the way down; another made two from the top of the keyhole to reach the bottom. A third account describes five rappels, but that is one party’s descent on two 25 m ropes rather than a list of fixed stations — which is why its lengths (about 23 m / 75 ft) look so precise and why its count disagrees with the others. That party’s final rappel off the southeast rib jammed and they sacrificed a rope; the standard line threads the low keyhole beneath the chockstone for a cleaner pull.

before.name: High Pass and the Gargett Mine, then the long sidehill under Larrabee to the South AmBo Saddle
before.notes:
Contamination warning before anything else: this is American Border Peak, 7,998 ft, in Washington. Canadian Border Peak is about a kilometre north across the international line and is a different mountain with its own routes, reached from British Columbia. Beta for the two is routinely mixed up because both are called 'Border Peak'. Everything here is the Washington approach from Twin Lakes.

From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft, take the High Pass Trail; at a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain — stay left, north. The trail contours the west side of Winchester, dips across Low Pass, and climbs to High Pass near 5,960 ft, about two miles and 750 ft of gain, where Mount Baker comes into view south.

At High Pass leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path north and west down to the old Gargett Mine workings around 5,400 ft. The mine creek is the last reliable water until lingering snow high on the peak.

From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks. This is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill of well over a mile across steep talus, scree, heather and brush.

Most parties camp at Gargett Basin or in the moraine bowl and climb from there rather than pushing summit day from the car.
before.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and never on wet grass or wet rock
hazards: Chronic rockfall — the defining hazard of this approach, helmets on from the Larrabee traverse
A long unmarked exposed sidehill on steep talus, scree, heather and brush
Wet grass or wet rock on the sidehill is a documented no-go condition
Two 60 m gullies of loose rock with climber-triggered rockfall onto the party below
Two to four rappels on descent off aged natural tat, with at least one recorded stuck and abandoned rope
before.baseFinding:
The 6,200-6,300 ft notch on Larrabee's northwest rib is the first gate, and the South Ambo Saddle at about 6,840 ft is the second. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

Between them is a red talus and moraine bowl. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

Arrival at the saddle: it is on the ridge crest directly south of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

Where the climbing actually starts is 200 yards above the saddle, not at it. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, then start traversing rightward on slabby red ledges. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft closely left of that rib.

De Gaulle's Nose is the aiming mark on the far side of the red face, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

And the hard condition rule: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Parties flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.

before: Hike east along the crest to a small col southwest of the North Ridge, then descend a 3rd-class gully down the north slope.
Set of stoppers, doubles from BD #0.3 to #2, plus a single #3.

Pitch 1 alone is 60m, so a 60m single rope is required just to reach the belay. Descent hikes east along the crest to a small col SW of the North Ridge, then a 3rd-class gully down the north slope - no rappelling, so no need for a second rope.

Climbs cracks up the northwest side of the buttress; begins on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the short crux on the 3rd pitch. Historically included a brief C1 aid section, though it may go free at the grade for strong parties. The route climbs cracks on the NW side of the buttress, starting on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the crux on pitch 3.
Hike east along the ridge crest to a small col southwest of the North Ridge, then descend a 3rd-class gully down the north slope.
Either walk southwest around Amphitheater Mountain back to Upper Cathedral Lake, or descend via a small col southwest of the North Ridge down a 3rd-class gully on the north slope.

Backpack in via Andrews Creek or Chewuch River trailheads to Upper Cathedral Lake (see West Route approach). From camp on the north side of Upper Cathedral Lake, walk about 15 minutes around the west side of the lake and scramble up to the base of the Ka'aba Buttress.

before.belay: Stand at the end of the roof where the triple crack system finishes.
before.notes: From the large block, follow the triple crack system to the end of a roof; belay there.

before.belay: Stand on the big sandy ledge at the top of the layback corner.
before.notes: Thin, exposed flake and layback moves to a sandy ledge belay.

before.belay: Stand on a large ledge above the twin handcrack.
before.notes: 'Money pitch' — right side of the sandy ledge up a right-facing finger-crack corner into a wild twin handcrack.
Stay left of the prow through a short low-angle offwidth corner section; multiple finish options.

before.name: Upper Cathedral Lake, round the west side of the water to the Ka'aba Buttress
before.notes:
Get to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by whichever of the long trails suits — this is the same basin used for Cathedral Peak, one to two days in from any trailhead.

The climbing is directly above the water, which is why every published approach time is measured in minutes rather than hours: ten to thirty minutes from camp. If you are camped on the north side of the lake, walk around it on the west side and straight up to the buttress.

Amphitheater's crags rise above the lake on the far side, and the two named buttresses on that wall are visible from your first sight of the water: Ka'aba on the left, Middle Finger on the right.
before.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Note the wall is north-west facing and stays in shade until around three in the afternoon, so an early start here is a cold one
hazards: A snow moat on the left side of the entry block into early July
The north-side descent gully holding firm snow through July
A north-west aspect that stays cold and shaded until mid-afternoon
Very remote — the nearest trailhead is a multi-day walk
before.baseFinding: The count is the test. Middle Finger Buttress is the biggest feature on the wall, and Ka'aba — where this route is — sits two buttresses to its left. So find the biggest one first, then count two left. Ka'aba itself is blocky and stepped, described as looking like stepping stones, which is quite unlike the clean sweep of Middle Finger. Be aware that the two buttresses between them are unnamed, so the count is the only handle you have — there is no known left-to-right inventory of this wall. Arrival is a large block at the base that you scramble onto for the first pitch, and getting onto it has a known seasonal trap. Approaching from the left side of the block runs into a large snow moat that stopped one party in early July. The right side goes, though it needs some care on friction moves crossing the top of the block to reach the wall. Walk-off, and there are two. The short one is a gully on the north side about a thousand feet east of Ka'aba, roughly thirty-five to forty degrees, giving a half-mile return to the lake — but it can hold firm snow through July. The longer one circles south around Amphitheater's western arm on sand and then meadows with a decent trail, rejoining the Boundary Trail and returning to the lake in about two miles and fifty minutes of easy walking.

before.notes: Use the fixed handline to reach the base of the corner, then climb the corner to the first belay. The easiest pitch of the route; save the thin cams for the next pitch.
A clean splitter finger crack. Double up on thin cams (Metolius blue and yellow sizes or equivalent), the sizes the crack takes for most of the pitch.
More splitter crack, easier and cruisey until a stiff finish at the top. A bolt now protects the exit where cams in pockets were once used.

A crimpy start leads to a crystal pocket and a small overlap, then excellent friction slab. Carry one 0.2 cam; the crux can be aided at roughly 5.10. From the ledge atop this pitch, an easy corner out left avoids the last pitch.
Tips splitter, only first-knuckle deep for about 20 ft, capped by a steep bolted finish. Descend by rappel; a single 60 m rope is enough.

before: From the Dosewallips Ranger Station (the road-walk/bike-in described separately covers reaching this point, since the Dosewallips River Road washout has closed vehicle access since 2002), pick up the Dosewallips River Trail and go about 1.4 miles to the signed junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail. Turn up the West Fork Trail and follow the river valley through old-growth forest roughly 8 miles to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft) — this is the last reliable flat camping and dependable water before the climb, though the West Fork ford here (and a second crossing near Diamond Meadow lower down) can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain, and the trail has substantial blowdown because NPS maintenance has lagged since the road closure. From Honeymoon Meadows continue up switchbacks about 1.2 more miles to Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the Dosewallips/Quinault divide and junction with the Enchanted Valley trail — roughly 16 miles and the end of maintained tread. At the pass, leave the trail and follow a climbers' boot path north over talus and heather benches about a mile and 700+ ft of gain to the Anderson Glacier moraine (~5,200 ft), passing a small tarn; this is the customary high camp. From the moraine, ascend along the glacier margin/moraine crest toward Flypaper Pass (6,500 ft), the notch between Mount Anderson to the east and 7,033-ft Echo Rock to the west — historically a steep snow finger, now increasingly bare scree and, late season, exposed ice as the finger has receded, making an ice axe/crampons and careful footing important; this section is best done in spring or early summer before it melts out. Anderson's Thumb is the prominent sandstone pinnacle in this Flypaper Pass/Echo Rock vicinity (visible from the Anderson Glacier basin around 5,250 ft); below the pass, bear west under Echo Rock and scramble talus and ledges to its base. No water is reliably available above the Anderson Glacier moraine besides snowmelt, so fill up at camp.

3 single-rope rappels, sometimes 4: one from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three down the gully just east of the top of the Northeast Couloir to the snow. Anchors are natural and may need rigging. Some parties instead make two rappels down slabs north of the east gully and traverse a wet ledge into it.

From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band and make a single rappel to the ledge on the southeast face; you may need to rig a natural anchor, and one party used a slung tree there. Then head over to the top of the Northeast Couloir and find the gully just east of it: two or three single-rope rappels down that gully reach the snow slopes below. Anchors are natural and not reliably in place, so carry webbing and nuts to build them. Alternatively, some parties make two rappels down the slabs just north of the east gully, off slings around blocks and a small tree, then traverse a wet, snow-covered ledge into the gully. Either way, finish with a roughly 2,500 ft glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to the lake, then out via the Colchuck Lake trail. Another option drops via a different gully into Porcupine Creek Basin with a traverse around Colchuck Peak.

before.notes: This table follows the southeast-face ledge line. The other descent makes two rappels down slabs just north of the east gully and then traverses a wet ledge into it. Choose one line before you leave the summit.
before.anchor: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and one earlier party describes rappelling from a slung tree on the southeast-facing ledge. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
hazards: No reliable fixed station — arriving expecting one and finding nothing is the failure mode here
You are committing off the summit onto a face on the opposite side of the peak from the couloir you climbed
before.station: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.

before.anchor: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description used a stopper anchor part way up the southeast face.
hazards: Gully terrain, loose
Anchors may have to be built from nuts and left behind
before.station: First of the rappels down the gully lying east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, entered from the southeast-face ledge.

before.notes: A third rappel in this gully is described as sometimes necessary, so treat the count as two or three here rather than fixed.
hazards: Loose gully; the transition onto snow at the bottom may need axe and crampons depending on season
before.station: Continues down the same gully; the sequence ends on the snow slopes below, from which parties traverse toward the Colchuck-Dragontail notch or glissade the Colchuck Glacier.

before.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
before.directions: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway near milepost 161, just west of Washington Pass, at about 5,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

before.name: Concord Tower summit
before.directions: Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 mi to a small meadow and take the climbers' path that branches left just past a small stream. Follow it up slabs, talus and meadow to the steep, loose gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower and climb it to the notch on Concord's north side, where the climbing starts; the route leads from there to the summit.

before: From Eldorado camp, traverse the Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col, pass through the col, and follow the north ridge along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where climbers rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier. From there, 4th and easy 5th class climbing for about 150 ft gains the sub-summit; a further short pitch (roughly 50 ft of contrived low 5th class climbing on loose rock) on the summit tower reaches the true summit.

before.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH
before.note: Large pullout at mile 20 of Cascade River Road; cross the Cascade River on a log/flagged crossing to the climbers' trail.
before.directions: From Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road south about 20 miles to the parking area near mile 20 — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard after that. Any overnight needs a free North Cascades backcountry permit, reserved in advance on Recreation.gov or drawn from the walk-up allocation in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

before.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp
before.note: High camp on the Inspiration Glacier flat used as base for Eldorado's satellite peaks.
before.directions: Backtrack a short distance along the road from the lot to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River — historically a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts from year to year. On the far side a steep, unmaintained climbers' path gains 3,000-3,500 ft through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek and opens into the meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, then continues onto glacier to the camp on the Inspiration flat. Figure 5-6 hours from the car, with roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear needed above the meadows.

before.name: Klawatti col
before.note: Break in the ridge above the McAllister Glacier; rappel ~75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier.
before.directions: Rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier northeast at roughly 7,800 ft, continuing well past Eldorado's own summit and the Tepeh Towers to the col on Klawatti's flank. Pass through the col and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper reaches of the McAllister Glacier to the break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft.

before.name: Klawatti Glacier crevasses
before.note: Traverse high and left across the crevassed Klawatti Glacier toward Austera.
before.directions: Work through the moat below the break — usually straightforward by August, more of a problem early season or in a heavy snow year — then rappel about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier. Leave a retrievable cordelette rather than fixed gear, since the exit reverses this pitch on lead at about 5.5. Rope up again and traverse the glacier high and climber's left toward Austera; the Klawatti has receded a great deal, so expect the crossing to be more broken than older descriptions suggest, and the peak itself does not resolve until you are close.

before.name: Austera Peak
before.note: Final 30 ft of low 5th-class climbing on the northeast face.
before.directions: Leave the glacier where the traverse runs out below the peak and scramble a few hundred feet of 4th class, then trend and traverse left along a broken ridge to the sub-summit. A final short pitch of well-protected low 5th class swings right onto the northeast face to the true summit; the rock on the summit tower is loose enough to be worth belaying.

before.notes: Pass through Klawatti col and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier to a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft. Cross the moat and rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier from an old anchor. Getting back up on the return is a short belayed pitch graded 5.5–5.6 (stay left in the gully), so carry a small rack and retrievable cord.

Traverse the Klawatti Glacier high and to the left toward Austera, which only comes into view when you are close. The route has moderate snow traverses and humps above and around crevasses, and icefalls below shed serac avalanches, so keep the line high and stay roped.

Leave packs and crampons at the rock. One line climbs a few hundred feet of 4th class, traverses left on a broken ridge, and finishes with about 30 ft of low 5th around to the right on the northeast face, which can be soloed or simul-climbed. An easier class 3 line on the southeast ridge also reaches this sub-summit, where most parties stop.

The true summit is a separate tower a few feet higher than the sub-summit. It is about 50 ft of contrived technical climbing on very poor rock and is rarely climbed. It needs a rope and careful rock testing; most parties judge the sub-summit a finished ascent.

before.name: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
before.notes: This is the same day out as the Southwest Ridge route on this peak and the two describe substantially the same ground. From the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,600 ft, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col. Tepeh Towers are passed along this same traverse. From the col, follow the ridge line along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where the standard sequence is a rappel of about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier, then a traverse high and left across it toward Austera. This is meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado, and it is worth saying plainly: this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak, despite the catalog filing several of these objectives out of the same area. Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête, not a free-standing summit, and it is the most accessible top in that group — which is exactly why parties end up on the wrong one.
before.season: Aug is the usual window; the timing is set by the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers being safely negotiable rather than by the rock
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glacier traverses
A moat at the rappel point that has to work in both directions
Loose rock on the final summit tower
Rime or verglas on the final chimney even in summer
Exposed climbing on the closing pitches above a remote glacier, with a long retreat
before.baseFinding:
The base is a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft that you rappel into, not walk through. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

Get there by counting, not by sighting Austera. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your left through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the second break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

Above the glacier traverse the climbing is short and countable: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a sub-summit, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the right on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

The false summit is the real hazard on this peak, and it is the test that matters. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. The true summit is reached only after crossing a narrow, often snowy ridge between two blocks and climbing a short chimney or a few feet of low fifth beyond it. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The moat beside the rappel point is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

before.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
before.note: Roadside pullout on Cascade River Road near mile 20; cross the Cascade River on a downstream log jam, then find the climbers' trail heading upstream on the far bank.
before.directions: Drive the Cascade River Road to the roadside pullout near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, and check the current road status first — flood damage near the park boundary has in some years added a bike or walk-in stretch to reach the actual trailhead. From the pullout, find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence and scout it before committing: it has been rebuilt repeatedly after floods and can be an awkward single log or a jam depending on the year.

before.name: Eldorado Creek Basin
before.note: Steep timbered climbers' trail and a boulder field top out in this alpine basin (roughly 5,500-5,800 ft) with reliable water from the creek and a waterfall; a common first-night camp.
before.directions: On the far bank pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path, which pushes through swampy brush and devil's club before settling into open old-growth timber. It gains roughly 1,500 ft through the trees, then breaks out onto the first of two wide boulder and talus fields — follow cairns and boot track for the path of least resistance through the rock rather than picking your own line.

before.name: Roush Creek Basin (Eldorado high camp)
before.note: Cross the connecting ridge near 6,100 ft and drop into Roush Creek Basin, the standard high camp (6,100-6,400 ft) at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier, with plentiful snowmelt water.
before.directions: Above the talus the path crosses an alpine meadow strewn with rocks and streams, then drops briefly. Cross the connecting ridge near 6,100 ft and drop into Roush Creek Basin at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Snowmelt water is plentiful here, which is why this is the standard high camp.

before.name: Inspiration Glacier (rope-up)
before.note: Rope up on the Eldorado Glacier and follow snowfields to the broad, flat Inspiration Glacier around 7,500 ft; large crevasses require zig-zag route-finding here.
before.directions: A slabby rock ramp leads from the basin onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier — rope up and put crampons on here, not higher. Follow snowfields up and onto the broad flat of the Inspiration. Crevasses are worst near Eldorado's east ridge, so stay roped, probe, and expect zig-zag route-finding; in flat light or whiteout, navigation across this open ice cap is genuinely hard and worth a compass bearing.

before.name: Klawatti Col / McAllister Glacier traverse
before.note: Contour the Inspiration Glacier north to Klawatti Col (~7,800 ft), then traverse a lobe of the McAllister Glacier below Klawatti Peak's West Face for about 0.4 mile.
before.directions: Contour north across the upper Inspiration to the col, then step through onto the McAllister Glacier and make a rising traverse east under Klawatti Peak's west face for about 0.4 mile. This is easy glacier travel by the standards of the day, but it is worth doing early while the snow bridges are still firm.

before.name: Klawatti-Austera Col
before.note: Late-season moat and crevasse gaps at this col can force Class 4-5 downclimbing at the lowest notch to gain Austera's south/southwest side.
before.directions: The traverse ends at a small notch at the base of Klawatti's north ridge, and getting down from it onto the Klawatti Glacier is the crux of the whole traverse. Early in the season it downclimbs; as the moat opens through the summer it needs a rappel of roughly 75 ft, and the lowest notch can push into class 5 with class 4 ground to its southeast. Old rappel anchors turn up here — treat any in-place tat as suspect and carry cord to back it up or replace it. On the way back, some parties climb well-protected rock out of the glacier rather than rig a rappel.

before.name: Austera Peak
before.note: True summit reached via 2-3 pitches of blocky rock on the South/Southwest Ridge ending in a short, often rime-covered 5.2 chimney.
before.directions: From the glacier, make another high traverse left across the upper Klawatti to the foot of Austera's southwest side, then drop packs and crampons. Broken, loose fourth-class rock leads up; a short cliff band above it is commonly bypassed on scree and ledges to the right rather than climbed direct. The finish is a chockstone chimney of about 60 ft — stemming and face moves on the left wall past roughly three jammed blocks — and a class 3+ ledge on the peak's east side avoids it entirely. Many parties stop at the easier sub-summit, because the last thirty feet of the true summit is loose.

before: From the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (River Bend Campground, ~2,700 ft, at the end of Lost River Road/FR 5400), follow the West Fork Methow River Trail roughly 8 miles up-valley to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) at Brush Creek. Turn left (south/west) on the PCT and follow it about 1.5-2 miles, crossing Jet Creek, to Horse Heaven Camp (~4,350 ft) — the last reliable, easy water before the climb (treat before drinking; flows can drop significantly by late season). From camp, pick up the old, unsigned Azurite Pass (Mill Creek) trail, which departs the PCT roughly 120 yards east of the Jet Creek crossing at a small rock cairn — easy to miss, and parties note the tread is faint/braided enough that a GPS track is genuinely useful here. The path switchbacks up through slide-alder brush, firms up into a real trail around 5,000 ft, re-crosses Jet Creek at about 5,300 ft (a rock-hop ford, can run high with snowmelt in June/early July), then climbs through eroded, brushy benches before breaking out into open heather meadows and granite slabs just below Azurite Pass (6,700 ft) — roughly 3-3.5 hours from Horse Heaven Camp. From the pass, leave the trail and work northeast/east up a mix of krummholz, sand, scree, and talus to a broad shoulder around 7,400 ft, then follow a gently rising, ducked/cairned traverse across a series of ribs, gullies, and sandy slopes toward the base of the summit tower. The final push climbs a prominent south/southwest-facing gully — loose underfoot (watch for rockfall onto party members below) but no harder than Class 3 in dry conditions; it can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is on the order of 12-13 miles with about 6,700 ft of gain, so most parties backpack in to Horse Heaven Camp and climb from there rather than doing it car-to-car.

before.name: Azurite Pass, the 7,400 ft shoulder and the west-face traverse
camps: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
before.notes: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
hazards: Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully; stay out of each other's fall line
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Two or three short snow runnels to cross on the west-face traverse
Many similar ribs and gullies; turning up too late puts you on the southwest face
Exposed class 3 on the traverse and summit gully
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge
before.baseFinding: Turn up too late and you meet the southwest face — that is the error to watch for. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the last gully to the south and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.

before.name: Harts Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail south

bivy.name: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
bivy.notes: This is the natural first night on the eastern approach to Azurite Pass and it breaks a walk that is otherwise too long to enjoy. From the trailhead near two thousand seven hundred feet the trail follows the West Fork Methow past Trout Creek and Brush Creek toward Jet Creek, and the camp sits partway along at about four thousand three hundred and fifty feet. Two warnings are worth taking seriously. The lower trail is overgrown and faint in places, though the tread improves as it climbs. And the brush on the banks of Jet Creek becomes extremely dense with no clear path through it at all, which is the section that costs parties hours and tempers. From here it is a sustained climb of well over two thousand feet to Azurite Pass and the peaks beyond, so leave early. Anyone weighing the two approaches should know they are about the same length and about equally neglected — pick by which side of the mountains you are driving from, not by hoping one has a better trail.
bivy.water: Creek water close at hand, reliable through the season. This is the last comfortable water before the long climb to the pass, so fill completely here.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed national forest camping — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the West Fork Methow trailhead. Fires only in an existing ring and only outside a burn ban, which by August usually means not at all.
bivy.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.

bivy.name: Azurite Pass
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

bivy.name: River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
bivy.notes: These are the staging camps for the eastern approach and the comfortable answer to the night before. From Winthrop the drive runs west on SR 20 and then up the Lost River Road through Mazama to the end of the pavement, continuing a mile and a half or so on the gravel of the Harts Pass road. The West Fork Methow trailhead sits close by at around two thousand seven hundred feet, at a wooden fence just off a short spur. Being low and in timber, they are usable well before and after the high country is in condition, and they are far enough down the road that none of the Harts Pass driving difficulties apply. They also make a sensible base for a party that wants a look at the trail before committing to it, which on this side is worth doing — the West Fork Methow tread is badly overgrown and in poor repair, and the brush on the banks of the upper creeks is dense enough that the trail effectively disappears.
bivy.water: The river is right there. Treat these as basic sites and assume you will filter rather than find a working spigot.
bivy.permit: No permit and no reservation, just a nightly fee paid on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a campsite, only to park at a trailhead. These are outside any wilderness, so none of the Pasayten self-issue paperwork applies.
bivy.capacity: Two small forested Forest Service campgrounds a short distance apart along the West Fork Methow, roughly eight to nine miles up the road from Mazama. Both are first come, first served only — there is no way to reserve and you must arrive in person to claim and pay for a site. Each is modest, so a summer weekend is a gamble.

before.notes: Start high at Harts Pass and follow the Pacific Crest Trail south to Horse Heaven Camp, where the old Mill Creek trail climbs to Azurite Pass. It avoids the lower West Fork Methow trail, which has been brushy and slow past its first few miles.
hazards: Long approach on the Pacific Crest Trail with a sustained climb to Azurite Pass
Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Exposed class 3 on the west-face traverse and summit gully
Route-finding among ribs and gullies on the upper slopes
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge

before.notes: From the Canyon Creek trailhead on SR-20, follow Canyon Creek to the Mill Creek trail and up past the old Azurite Mine to the west slopes of the peak or on to Azurite Pass. The Mill Creek trail is badly overgrown in places and route-finding through alder is slow, so most parties prefer the east-side starts.

Afternoon thunderstorms; no shelter near the pass

before.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead
before.note: This is the Anderson and Watson Lakes trailhead, the start of the long cross-country line past the Watson Lakes and Diobsud Lakes to the Diobsud Creek Glacier.
before.directions: From SR-20 near milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive about 14 mi to the Baker Dam turnoff. Cross the dam on FS Road 1106, turn left on FS Road 1107 and follow it 8 to 9 mi to a signed spur on the left, which ends at the Anderson and Watson Lakes Trailhead in about 1 mi. The road is long and rough; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

before.name: Wilderness-boundary saddle
before.note: Below this saddle the trail forks: right drops 0.5 mi to Lower Anderson Lake, left climbs here into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness. Leave the trail at the saddle for the boot path south along the ridge.
before.directions: Follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 through forest to the Anderson Butte Trail junction and stay left. Continue to the next junction, where the right fork drops to Lower Anderson Lake; bear left and climb to the saddle where the trail enters the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness.

before.name: Diobsud basin
before.note: The Diobsud Lakes basin, reached through heather below the 5,300 ft saddle on Mt. Watson's north side; the last dependable camp and water below the peak.
before.directions: From the saddle, follow the boot path south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake to Upper Anderson Lake, the last easy water. Angle northeast up a short wooded gully, cross the slabs, scree and snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side, go over a saddle near 5,300 ft and descend heather to the Diobsud Lakes.

before.name: Access gully to Diobsud Creek Glacier
before.note: Loose rock and slick dirt in the chute leading to the glacier's toe once snow has melted out — expect to claw up steep, loose dirt gullies here.
before.directions: From the basin, sidehill across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, then climb mossy slabs toward the steep, loose dirt-and-scree gullies that lead up to Bacon's south ridge.

before.name: Diobsud Creek Glacier crossing
before.note: Rope up here — crevasses open on the icecap by mid-to-late season; probe and stay roped through to the saddle below the summit block.
before.directions: Climb the steep, loose gully onto Bacon's south ridge, where broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here. When snow-filled the gully is avalanche terrain, and it goes far more easily on firm morning snow.

before.name: Bacon Peak
before.directions: Stay roped and probe across the glacier toward the summit block, then follow the flat, often windy summit ridge over a short snow arete and scramble the dry rocks to the summit.

before: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: down the summit snow slopes and col, back onto and down the Diobsud Creek Glacier (roped, same crevasse caution as the approach), down through the steep loose gully/south-ridge terrain to Diobsud Lakes, then back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead. This is a walk-off/glacier-descent — no rappels are used on the standard round trip; the technical difficulty is glacier travel and loose, steep downclimbing rather than anything requiring rope-anchored lowering. Parties continuing north as part of a longer Bacon-Hagan-Blum (or Watson-Bacon-Hagan-Blum) traverse instead descend from the summit down quick snow slopes to the "Bacon Tarns" (small glacial-melt ponds on a rock bench below the Green Lake Glacier), then follow heather and meadow along Bacon's north ridge, passing high above Green Lake toward Hidden Lake, continuing the traverse rather than returning to the Watson Lakes trailhead. Either way, expect the same loose-rock and brush hazards on the south-ridge gully in reverse, and re-assess glacier conditions/crevasse bridges on the return trip since afternoon snow softening changes the picture from the morning ascent.

before.name: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
before.notes: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle beyond the Lower Anderson Lake fork, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path running south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake. The path opens into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. Leave the lake heading northeast up a short wooded gully and continue that way onto open moraine and heather slopes near 5,300 ft. Traverse under the Watson peaks and drop to about 5,000 ft to get around a buttress on their east side, then climb to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross to the south side of the ridge. Continue east, losing a little height toward the next low point in the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, crossing a short buttress on easy ledges on the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.
hazards: No tread, no signage and no marked line above Upper Anderson Lake
Lingering snowfields on the traverse beneath the Watson peaks
Crevasse hazard on the icecap if the line drifts onto it
Featureless snow slopes near the top — navigation in whiteout is the real difficulty
before.baseFinding: The saddle sequence is the proof, and the heights go down before they go up. From the open moraine and heather at about 5,300 ft this line loses height twice: first to roughly 5,000 ft to get round the buttress east of the Watson peaks, then again beyond the 5,360 ft saddle, dropping toward a 4,900 ft saddle reached over a short buttress on easy ledges. A party that keeps gaining height through this stretch has stayed on the wrong side of the ridge — at the 5,360 ft saddle you cross to the south side, and remaining on the north side is the mistake. The camp lies at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of the summit, and from it the peak is gained by climbing southeast. The last test is what is under your feet: this line reaches the summit without crossing a glacier at all, so if the ground ahead is crevassed ice rather than a snow-covered slope, you have drifted onto the icecap and should rope up or come back to the walking line.

before.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead
before.note: NW Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk; boot path for the mountain starts behind the outhouse rather than on the main Barclay Lake trail.
before.directions: From US-2 near the town of Baring, follow gravel Barclay Creek Road (FR-6024) to its end at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and is self-issued at the kiosk.

before.name: Climber's-trail cairn off old logging road
before.note: Leave the abandoned logging road (walked ~1/3 mile from the lot) at a cairn where a rough, unmaintained boot path splits off toward the mountain's base.
before.directions: Do not start on the signed Barclay Lake trail — the climbers' path for the mountain leaves from behind the outhouse. Walk the old, abandoned logging road for about a third of a mile to the cairn, which is easy to walk straight past since nothing else marks the split.

before.name: Creek-side ascent gully
before.note: Boot path climbs steep, loose dirt slopes and crosses the small creek several times on the way toward the base of the north wall — stay near the water to keep the path.
before.directions: From the cairn the path pitches straight up steep, loose dirt beside the small creek that drains the face, crossing it several times on the way. The tread is faint and frequently lost in slide alder, vine maple and devil's club, so if you lose it, work back to the water rather than casting around on the slope.

before.name: Couloir Camp
before.note: Standard bivy for the multi-day face route, reached after ~1000 ft of steep forested/brushy hillside above the wall's base; historically fixed with rope to haul loads.
before.directions: Roughly another 1,200 ft of steep forested and brushy hillside above the creek section reaches the camp. It is the last flat ground before technical climbing, and the point where parties splitting the approach into two days bivy and gear up.

before.name: Snow-filled summit couloir
before.note: The next 1300 ft climbs two parallel rock ribs separated by a large couloir that holds snow into August; four ~300-400 ft rock steps here demand sustained grade V-VI climbing on loose, vegetated rock.
before.directions: Above camp the ground rises between two precipitous parallel ribs of cliff and brush that flank the couloir. Follow the left rib until it joins another rib further left, then traverse rightward along ledges to the foot of the first rock step. The couloir holds snow well into August in a normal year, so carry an axe for this section early in the season.

before.name: Baring Mountain summit
before.note: True summit at the top of the face; descend the non-technical south/back side (west-ridge/talus basin) rather than reversing the wall.
before.directions: Four vertical steps of roughly 300, 400, 220 and 250 ft, separated by spacious ledges, lead to the summit ridge. The second step is the crux, with 120-degree roof sections, delicate vertical climbing and protection poor enough that the first ascent resorted to aid and bolts; parties commonly bivy on the ledge above it. A few hundred feet of scrambling above the last step tops out. Do not plan on reversing the wall — the accepted way down is the non-technical walk-off on the far side of the mountain, and no fixed rappel stations should be assumed anywhere on the face.
