before.belay: The full-length pitch ends by stepping left to an anchor; the shorter variant stops earlier at an anchor on a ledge.
before.notes: Arch feature with natural gear to ledge anchor; full pitch continues past bolts through shallow groove, tricky stemming, cruxy knobs section, moves left to anchor.
Thin ramp then stemming corner with knobs to a testy balance crux high up; 3 bolts plus small gear for crux.

before.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail 674)
before.note: End of FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) off Mt. Baker Highway; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk, and this is the start of the long multi-day approach toward Bear Creek.
before.directions: Drive the Mount Baker Highway to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and follow it to the road end at about 3,100 ft, where Hannegan Pass Trail #674 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk here.

before.name: Hannegan Pass
before.note: Broad meadow saddle where Hannegan Pass Trail meets the Chilliwack River Trail; leave the maintained tread here and drop north into the Chilliwack River valley toward Canada.
before.directions: Follow Trail #674 up the valley, nearly level for the first mile and then at a steady grade, roughly 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the broad meadow saddle of the pass. Figure 2.5 to 3 hours.

before.name: Bear Creek Camp (Chilliwack River Trail)
before.note: Established camp at the Bear Creek confluence on the Chilliwack River Trail, the jump-off point for the Bear Mountain approach; NPS closed this camp after the 2021 Bear Creek Fire, so verify current access before counting on it.
before.directions: Drop off the east side of the pass and continue about 5 miles down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the national park boundary where the Chilliwack River Trail proper begins. The tread loses elevation past U.S. Cabin camp to the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-cable car and a serious ford in high water, then runs down-valley past the Copper Creek and Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8 to 9 hours from the car. Check current status of the Bear Creek camp, which the Park Service closed after the 2021 fire.

before.name: Meadows above Ruta Lake
before.note: From Bear Creek, climb steep timber then huckleberry slopes east to treeline; the route gains the divide crest in open meadowland just above Ruta Lake.
before.directions: Leave the maintained trail at Bear Creek and ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing during snowmelt. Climb east into steep, brushy timber; higher the brush gives way to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows at about 5,800 ft above Ruta Lake.

before.name: NW Ridge saddle high camp (6,480')
before.note: Traverse loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822, crossing a rock rib, to this saddle on Bear's NW ridge — the standard bivy for the North Buttress, roughly 21 miles and two days from the trailhead.
before.directions: Traverse the divide from the meadows, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to the broad saddle at 6,480 ft on Bear's northwest ridge. This is the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites, about 21 miles from the trailhead, usually reached on the second day.

before.name: Glacier couloir base below North Buttress
before.note: About 1.5 hours below camp; loose rock and occasional icefall/rockfall off the shrinking glacier remnant in the couloir make early starts and helmets essential here.
before.directions: The route begins by losing height: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle and cross several minor gullies to the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the north buttress, about 60 to 90 minutes. An axe and crampons are worth their weight here even in summer. Loose rock and occasional icefall out of the shrinking glacier make an early start and helmets the norm.

before.name: Bear Mountain summit
before.note: True summit horn gained via seven pitches of 5.10 climbing up the buttress above the couloir; descend west on the south side of the crest, then downclimb a short 3rd-class gully back toward the saddle camp.
before.directions: Climb the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into the slabs leading to the corner system where the technical climbing starts, watching for a moat where the snow meets rock. Seven pitches up to 5.10a follow the crest, with the off-width crux on pitch four and easier alternatives on the crest, to the top of the buttress; a scramble from there gains the true summit.
